scope: Guide-only specimens; no Explore population or placement changes.

speciesText.name: Textile cone
marks: Smooth, tapered shell with a pointed spire at the broad end
Brown lines form a fine net around many pale triangular patches
One long, narrow opening runs along the side of the shell
A pale muscular foot with brown mottling extends beneath the shell
speciesText.role: A predator of other marine snails that searches sand, rubble and reef surfaces for prey.
speciesText.fact: It hunts using a hollow tooth that injects venom. A beautiful shell can still hold a living animal; observe it without handling it.

marineProfile.habitat: Indo-Pacific reefs, sandy areas and coral rubble, often beneath rocks. The Conus Biodiversity Website records it from the intertidal zone to about 50 m deep.
marineProfile.diet: Mainly other sea snails, including cowries and other cone snails.
marineProfile.behavior: Moves on a muscular foot, usually sheltering by day and hunting at night. A flexible siphon draws water into the mantle cavity.
marineProfile.observe: Rotate to find the long opening, then compare the low spire and tapered shape with the giant triton. The giant clam instead has two hinged shells.

evidence.taxonomy: WoRMS lists Conus textile Linnaeus, 1758 as the accepted species; Cylinder textile is represented under Conus textile.
evidence.conservation: LC is explicitly reported by Qatar e-Nature and corroborated by a 2024 Frontiers review. The direct IUCN page and DOI were inaccessible. Secondary citations identify a 2013 assessment, but that year was not verified from the assessment itself, so iucnYear is null rather than guessed.
evidence.morphology: Michigan account supports tapered convex shell, moderate pointed spire, aperture, triangular network, soft-part coloration and spiral bands. Qatar account independently supports shell form and typical adult size. Pattern and colour vary; model is an illustrative typical form.
evidence.ecology: Michigan supports intertidal to about 50 m, sand/rubble/rock habitat and predominantly gastropod prey. Queensland Museum explicitly calls the species a mollusc-eater. Do not repeat the Lizard Island Field Guide fish-eating shorthand or the Qatar account main-diet wording: these conflict with the more detailed monograph and museum classification.
evidence.behavior: Qatar e-Nature supports sheltering during the day and nocturnal hunting. Australian Museum cone-shell guide supports the muscular foot and venomous tooth. DORIS species account describes the siphon as respiratory; no swimming or shell flexing is implied.

model.notes: Typical 9 cm shell, within published 40–150 mm range and reported adult 9–10 cm. Keep the hard shell fixed; modest local siphon/soft-body movement is illustrative. Shell aperture belongs on the underside-facing side of a crawling animal; do not add two hinged valves.

evidence.comparisons: Giant triton and giant clam are broad body-plan comparisons available in the current guide, not close taxonomic lookalikes. They distinguish one low-spired shell, one tall-spired shell and two hinged valves.

speciesText.name: Orange cup coral (sun coral)
marks: A cluster of tube-shaped cups rises from a shared hard base
Red or orange tissue covers the cups
Fine yellow tentacles form a ring around each central mouth
Many small polyps make a rounded mound rather than long branches
speciesText.role: A colony of small predators that catches drifting animal plankton. It grows on hard surfaces without building a large reef framework.
speciesText.fact: It has no photosynthetic algae living in its tissues, so it can feed and grow in shaded places. Introduced populations can compete with native corals in the Atlantic.

marineProfile.habitat: Shaded rock, overhangs and artificial surfaces. Native to the Indo-Pacific and eastern Pacific; introduced in parts of the Atlantic. Smithsonian reports it at depths down to 60 m.
marineProfile.diet: Tiny drifting animals, called zooplankton, caught by the tentacles.
marineProfile.behavior: Polyps often extend their tentacles at night to feed, then draw them back into their hard cups. New polyps can bud from the colony.
marineProfile.observe: Look for a separate mouth and ring of tentacles in each cup. Compare this colony with the magnificent anemone's single large oral disc and the cauliflower coral's knobbly branches.

evidence.taxonomy: WoRMS World List of Scleractinia lists accepted Tubastraea coccinea Lesson, 1830. ITIS, Smithsonian and several older ecological sources use 1829. The product scientific name does not include an authority year; the difference is documented here.
evidence.conservation: Aquarium of the Pacific explicitly says the species has not been evaluated by IUCN; SeaLifeBase independently lists Not Evaluated (N.E.). Use NE and null year. Do not mistake Singapore national DD status or an invasive-species impact classification for the global IUCN extinction-risk category.
evidence.morphology: USGS supports orange/red polyp tissue, yellow/orange tentacles and rounded 14 cm colonies. Smithsonian specifies cups up to 11 mm diameter, projection up to 4 cm, a white skeleton under the tissue and variable spacing. Four marks describe the illustrated compact colony rather than imply all colonies share identical spacing.
evidence.ecology: Smithsonian documents native Indo-Pacific/eastern-Pacific distribution, introduction into the Atlantic, zooplankton feeding, absence of symbiotic algae and a non-reef-building habit. Its Ecology text reports down to 60 m, while the parameters table records a 78 m Louisiana observation. The profile attributes 60 m to that account and does not claim it is an absolute limit.
evidence.behavior: Aquarium of the Pacific supports usual nighttime tentacle extension; Smithsonian supports budding of new polyps. Flexible tentacle motion is a gentle illustrative current response, while the calcareous cups and placement root remain fixed.
evidence.caveat: The Smithsonian page has an inconsistent Primary Producer database label and a later hermatypic typo. Its detailed Ecology/Life History descriptions and the other sources agree this animal lacks photosynthetic algae and captures prey; the proposed copy follows those descriptions.

model.notes: Use a small mound with distinct short cups, orange-red tissue, pale-yellow tapered tentacles and visible central mouths. Keep cups rigid and gently sway only flexible tentacles. A 14 cm colony is a cited common upper size, not a universal biological maximum.

evidence.comparisons: Magnificent anemone and cauliflower coral are useful introductory body-plan contrasts, not close species-level lookalikes. No species name is included in any field-mark clue.
